whatItIs: A single-author Agent Skills plugin containing 16 hand-written editorial rule sets, one per published house style (GOV.UK, Google dev docs, GitLab, GitHub, Kubernetes, MDN, Red Hat, 18F, Microsoft, Mailchimp, Apple HIG writing, CDC Clear Communication, NHS, SEC Plain English, W3C Manual of Style, NASA STI). Each lives at skills/<name>/SKILL.md (65-82 lines, 1171 lines total) plus agents/openai.yaml and references/provenance.md or references/SOURCE.md. The only executable code is scripts/validate_repo.py (437 lines), a structural linter for the repo itself. No evals, no scoring, no test corpus — scripts/validate_repo.py:390 actively fails the build if an `evals/` directory exists, and AGENTS.md:9 says "Keep model eval infrastructure out of v0.2."
method: Pick one stylebook by artifact and audience, then let it govern structure and prose while facts stay frozen. Every one of the 16 files is cut to the same skeleton: a "Protect/Preserve <domain> truth" section that forbids changing numbers, legal conditions, code or clinical thresholds; a numbered planning section that forces the writer to name the reader, their decision and the minimum facts that decision needs; two or three sections of imperative prose rules (what goes first, which sentence subject, how a procedure is shaped, what an error message must contain); an "## Avoid" list; and a "## Final pass" self-check. All 16 contain "## Avoid" and "## Final pass" (measured: those two lines are the only body lines shared by all 16; max pairwise vocabulary Jaccard 0.31, median 0.19 over 120 pairs — so the skeleton is shared but the prose is genuinely written per style, not templated). Selection is a human judgement supported by two tables: README.md:33-48 maps "I am writing…" to a skill, and STYLE-MATRIX.md:6-22 gives each skill a primary audience, a "primary optimization", a distinctive behavior and an avoid column. README.md:118 says use one primary stylebook unless a hybrid is explicitly needed. Provenance is the repo's real obsession: PROVENANCE.md classifies each source A/B/C, each references/SOURCE.md carries "Operationalized:" and "Not copied:" lines (see skills/w3c-technical-reports/references/SOURCE.md:13-20), and CONTRIBUTING.md:5-12 refuses any source that is "a short list of generic writing advice" or that lacks a documented licence decision.
measures: It measures itself, not documents. scripts/validate_repo.py checks frontmatter shape (only `name` and `description`, line 135), that the description contains the literal string "Use for" (line 144), a 500-line and 50 KB per-skill budget (lines 148, 153), SHA-256 pins on the original 11 SKILL.md files so they cannot drift (lines 43-55, 156-160), relative-link integrity (lines 307-317), the A/B provenance counts (line 336), and a forbidden-placeholder sweep (lines 403-423). Nothing reads a user's document and returns a number. No reader is simulated, no answer key exists, no before/after is compared. The 16 "## Final pass" sections (extracted all of them) are same-author self-checks phrased "confirm that the reader can identify X, Y, Z" — no fresh reader, no score, no pass/fail count. COMPATIBILITY.md:43-48 states it plainly: "Discovery is not behavioral certification… v0.2 does not include multi-model A/B evals". The sharpest fact: the one source that is an actual scored instrument, the CDC Clear Communication Index (20 questions, scored), was deliberately stripped of its scoring — PROVENANCE.md:44-45 "operationalized without reproducing its 20 questions, scoring thresholds, score sheets"; skills/cdc-clear-communication/references/SOURCE.md:16 "Not copied: the Index questions, scoring method, score sheets"; and skills/cdc-clear-communication/SKILL.md:72 even forbids "copying a checklist score into the output as proof". So this repo converted the only measurement available to it into prose, for licensing reasons. That is the opposite direction from terse.
weaknesses: Pure prescription with a self-check at the end, and the repo says so itself (COMPATIBILITY.md:43-48, AGENTS.md:9, scripts/validate_repo.py:390). Nothing shows that picking `govuk` over `microsoft-writing-style` changes any outcome, or that a stylebook beats an unguided rewrite — exactly the comparison terse already ran and that published standards lost. 16 overlapping rule sets, a "use one primary" rule, and no way to check the choice was right. Three commits, one release, one unrelated issue, single author, no fork traffic; nothing has stress-tested the rules in public. The "Final pass" asks the same model that just wrote the text whether a reader could follow it — the curse-of-knowledge failure mode terse has a whole pass for. Provenance rigour is real but it is legal hygiene, not quality evidence, and it is what cost the repo its one measuring instrument. To its credit it avoids two things terse already rejected: there are no hard per-sentence word limits anywhere in the 16 files (grepped; the only "at most" is about humour) and no linter or CI punctuation gate over prose.

transferable.approach: Fact-preservation map as a revise regression guard: before rewriting, inventory every fact, number, qualification and conditional from the source doc; after rewriting, map each one to its location in the new text and compare numbers independently from prose; any item that lost scope or a qualifier is a defect.
transferable.whereItLives: skills/sec-plain-english/SKILL.md:51-55 ('## Test the rewrite'), restated as a user-facing artifact at EXAMPLES.md:103
transferable.whyItMightWork: terse measures whether readers can answer questions, which catches findability and placement well, but a fact dropped or softened during revise is only caught if some question happened to probe it. The map is a cheap checkable table, not an opinion: each row either resolves to a location in the rewrite or it does not. It is the same failure class as terse's 'lie', but detected on the write side rather than the read side.
transferable.collidesWith: Additive to revise pass 4 (repair) and to the bake-off scoring; no collision. It does compete for judge attention in the 3-writer 2-judge bake-off, so it belongs as a precondition every candidate must satisfy before judging, not as a judged criterion.

transferable.approach: Per-genre question-slot bank: a checklist of question archetypes by artifact type (success signal, cleanup, recovery from error, prerequisite timing, version/feature state, cost, duration, what can go wrong, next action) used to test whether the code-derived question set has coverage gaps.
transferable.whereItLives: The 16 '## Final pass' sections, e.g. skills/govuk/SKILL.md:64-68, skills/google-developer-docs/SKILL.md:70, skills/kubernetes-docs/SKILL.md:60, skills/github-docs/SKILL.md:66, skills/18f-content/SKILL.md:60
transferable.whyItMightWork: terse derives its answer key from the code, which is the right ruler, but question *selection* is still an unguided act and can miss a whole category the code can answer and the docs never did. This is 16 pre-written, MIT-licensed slates of 4-6 slots each, usable as a coverage audit on the generated questions rather than as writing advice: 'the code answers "how do I verify it worked" — did any of my six questions ask that?'
transferable.collidesWith: Touches audit's question-generation step. It must stay a coverage check applied after questions are derived from the code; if it became the question source, it would reintroduce the standards-produce-audits failure and would generate questions the code cannot answer.

transferable.approach: Testable-rule gate on terse's own fixed writing rules: every rule must name an observable decision (what goes first, which sentence subject, what information an error must contain) and a rule that reduces to an adjective is rejected.
transferable.whyItMightWork: It is a falsifiable property of a rule's phrasing, checkable by a fresh reader without running the chain, and it is a plausible partial explanation for why the five published standards lost: standards mostly assert qualities ('be clear', 'be professional') that an auditor can score but a rewriter cannot execute. Worth testing as a hypothesis, not adopting as doctrine.
transferable.collidesWith: revise pass 2 (fixed writing rules). It is a meta-rule about how those rules are phrased, so it constrains that pass rather than replacing it. The 16 SKILL.md bodies themselves must NOT be adopted there — they are a second, larger, competing rule set of exactly the already-rejected kind.

transferable.approach: Pin the plugin's own instruction files by SHA-256 in a validator, with a per-skill line and byte budget, so a cleanup commit cannot silently change measured behavior.
transferable.whyItMightWork: terse's 3-right-to-6-right result is attached to a specific wording of audit and revise. A pin makes any edit to those files an explicit, reviewed act and forces a re-measurement, which is the only honest way to keep the claim attached to the artifact.
transferable.collidesWith: Nothing in the method; it is repo hygiene for terse itself. Low value, and it fights routine editing, so it is worth it only for files whose exact wording a published measurement depends on.
